How StegPony works, and its limits
Read this before relying on it

StegPony encrypts a message or file and hides it in the fine detail of a photo, or in text. The photo still looks and opens like any other. Without the right passphrase or key, there is nothing to find: no header, no marker, and no way to tell an image with something hidden from one without.\n\nPassphrases are stretched with Argon2id, keys use X25519 (the same keys as age), and the content is sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305. Every image and every text has room for two hidden messages; the second is either your decoy or random filler, so the two cases look the same.

Send the file exactly as StegPony saved it: as a file or document attachment, by email, or through a service that keeps files unchanged. Anything that re-encodes the picture destroys what\'s hidden. That includes most messengers\' photo mode, resizing, editing, filters, and some cloud and social services. Telegram photos are an experimental exception, described below.\n\nNever send or post the original photo as well. Anyone holding both can compare them.

Telegram on an iPhone normally shrinks a photo to 1280 pixels on the long side and recompresses it at a fixed quality. With Telegram photo from an iPhone chosen, StegPony makes that copy itself before hiding anything, and tones down very bright or very dark patches slightly, so Telegram should have little left to change. The copy is usually smaller than your photo, so it holds less.

This is experimental. In early lab tests, messages prepared this way came through Telegram with both hidden messages intact, but copies made by the app itself are not verified yet, and Telegram can change how it handles photos in any update. Pick the saved photo from Telegram's photo gallery and send it in standard quality, not HD, one per message. A photo attached as a file, or shared into Telegram from another app, can be recompressed differently, which destroys what's hidden. Send one to yourself first and open the downloaded photo in StegPony. The detectability rating describes the image as saved; it hasn't been measured for photos after Telegram.

Telegram on Android, and WhatsApp and Signal, change photos in ways a prepared copy can't avoid: tests found small changes all over the picture, which destroy what's hidden. For them, send the image as a file.

The best cover is a photo you take just for this, with StegPony\'s camera or your own, that has never been shared anywhere. Use each photo once. StegPony warns when a photo was used before, or looks like a download or a messenger copy.\n\nJPEG mode keeps the photo a JPEG with your camera\'s own compression, which is what photos from a phone normally are. Lossless mode saves a PNG; use it for images that were PNGs to begin with.

Text holds far less than a photo and is easier to notice, so use it when a photo can't be sent. What's hidden is encrypted the same way, with the same passphrases, keys and decoy.

Words: the hidden data becomes a run of ordinary words that reads as nonsense. It gets past automated filters and a quick look, not a person who reads it. Even a short message takes over 130 words, because every text has room for a decoy. Capitals, punctuation and line breaks can change on the way; a changed, missing or added word can't.

Invisible characters: the hidden data becomes characters that don't show, tucked into a message you write. It is weak. Many apps, websites and keyboards remove these characters, and anyone who looks for them finds them at once. Send a test to yourself through the same app before relying on it.

The rating says how hard the result should be to tell apart from an untouched photo, based on how much is hidden for the size and detail of the photo. Low, Medium and High come from tests with a standard detector on real phone photos, and are set below what those tests showed, because better detectors exist.\n\nLow is a good aim. Keep messages short, and use a large, detailed photo for files. A high rating doesn\'t mean the content can be read; it means someone looking for hidden content has a better chance of noticing that something is there.

A passphrase protects the message only as well as it resists guessing. Use several random words, not something about you, and share it in person or over a channel you trust.\n\nWith a public key there is no shared secret: you hide for someone\'s age1… key, and only their secret key opens it. A Curve25519 OpenPGP key from PGPony or GnuPG works the same way. StegPony keeps your secret keys encrypted on this phone; it never stores passphrases.

An OpenPGP hardware key (YubiKey, Nitrokey, Token2) with a Curve25519 (cv25519) decryption key can open images hidden for it, over NFC or USB. The key does the key exchange itself, so its secret never leaves it. You enter the key\'s PIN each time; StegPony doesn\'t keep it. RSA keys can\'t be used.

A decoy is a second message under a second passphrase. If someone forces you to open an image or a text, give them the decoy. Nobody can tell from it whether a decoy exists, and StegPony gives the same answer for a wrong passphrase as for an image with nothing in it.\n\nThe limit: someone who knows StegPony knows everything it hides has room for two messages, and may not believe there is only one. Make the decoy believable, and on your own phone type its passphrase rather than leaving the field empty, which would try your own keys.

StegPony has no network access. Your keys and contacts are encrypted with a key held in Android\'s secure hardware, and are left out of backups and phone transfers. Screenshots are blocked on Reveal and Keys, and copied messages leave the clipboard after a minute.\n\nThe app lock and the launcher disguise slow down a casual look at your phone. They don\'t hide that StegPony is installed: its real name still shows in Android\'s app settings.
